questions.q: 'Absolute ownership' of land, as distinguished from 'limited ownership' (such as tenancy or lease), refers to:
o: Ownership subject to a fixed time period only
Full, unrestricted title and rights over the land, including the right to possess, use, and dispose of it, subject only to general law
A right that automatically expires after 99 years
Only government-held land
questions.src: Settled land law classification — absolute ownership carries the fullest bundle of rights over property, distinguished from limited/qualified interests like tenancy or leasehold

questions.q: The 'Doctrine of Eminent Domain' refers to:
o: The right of a private citizen to acquire any land forcibly
The inherent sovereign power of the State to acquire private property for public purpose, subject to payment of compensation as prescribed by law
A doctrine that prohibits the State from ever acquiring private land
A rule applicable only to agricultural land
questions.src: Settled constitutional/land law doctrine — eminent domain is the state's power to compulsorily acquire private property for public use, subject to legal safeguards including compensation

questions.q: The 'Doctrine of Escheat' applies when:
o: A landowner voluntarily gifts land to the government
A person dies intestate (without a will) and without any legal heirs, in which case the property reverts/passes to the State
Land is acquired through eminent domain
A tenant fails to pay rent for one year
questions.src: Settled land law doctrine — escheat is the reversion of property to the State when an owner dies without a will and without legal heirs to inherit

questions.q: 'Bona Vacantia' (ownerless goods/property) as a legal doctrine is closely related to escheat and refers to:
o: Property that is jointly owned by multiple co-owners
Property that has no owner (e.g., of a dissolved company with no claimants, or unclaimed property) and which, in the absence of any rightful claimant, vests in the State
Property under a valid, enforceable lease
Property currently under mortgage
questions.src: Settled doctrine — bona vacantia (masterless/ownerless goods) is property without any identifiable owner, which vests in the State in the absence of a rightful claimant, distinct from but related to escheat

questions.q: The Telangana Rights in Land and Pattadar Pass Books Act, 2020 primarily deals with:
o: Regulation of urban commercial leases
Maintenance of land records, issue of Pattadar Pass Books/Title Deeds, and updating of Records of Rights for agricultural land in Telangana
Only industrial land allotment
Interpretation of central tax statutes
questions.src: Telangana Rights in Land and Pattadar Pass Books Act, 2020 — governs maintenance of land records, Pattadar Pass Books, and Records of Rights (ROR) for agricultural land in the state

questions.q: The 'Torrens System' of land titling, referenced in comparative land law discussions, is primarily known for providing:
o: No documentation of title at all
A government-guaranteed, conclusive title to registered land, intended to eliminate the need for repeated title verification with each transaction
Title only to movable property
A system exclusively used for leasehold interests
questions.src: Torrens System (originating in Australia, referenced for comparative title-guarantee/title-insurance discussion) — provides state-guaranteed conclusive title upon registration, reducing reliance on chain-of-title verification

questions.q: The 'Zamindari Settlement' (Permanent Settlement) system, introduced during British rule, primarily involved:
o: Direct settlement of land revenue between the government and individual cultivators
Recognition of Zamindars (intermediaries) as owners of land who collected revenue from cultivators/tenants and paid a fixed sum to the government
Complete abolition of private land ownership
A system used only in Madras Presidency
questions.src: Settled land reform history — the Zamindari/Permanent Settlement (introduced by Cornwallis, 1793) created a class of intermediary landlords (Zamindars) responsible for revenue collection, later abolished post-independence

questions.q: The 'Ryotwari Settlement' system, as distinguished from the Zamindari system, primarily involved:
o: Settlement of land revenue directly between the government and the individual cultivator (ryot), without any intermediary Zamindar
The same intermediary structure as the Zamindari system
A system applicable only to forest land
Complete elimination of land revenue
questions.src: Settled land reform history — the Ryotwari system involved direct revenue settlement between the state and individual cultivators (ryots), without zamindar intermediaries, prevalent in parts of Madras and Bombay Presidencies

questions.q: The 'Mahalwari System' of land revenue settlement, as distinguished from Zamindari and Ryotwari, was characterised by:
o: Settlement made with an entire village or estate (mahal) as a unit, with joint responsibility for revenue payment among the village community/landholders
Settlement exclusively with the British Crown directly
A system applied only to coastal regions
Complete abolition of any revenue obligation
questions.src: Settled land reform history — the Mahalwari system settled revenue with a village or estate (mahal) as a collective unit, distinct from the individual-cultivator Ryotwari and intermediary-based Zamindari systems

questions.q: Post-independence land reform legislation in India generally aimed to abolish Zamindari, Jagirs, and Inams primarily in order to:
o: Increase the number of intermediaries between the state and cultivators
Eliminate intermediary landlord classes and establish direct relationship between the State and the actual tiller/cultivator of the land, furthering land reform objectives
Transfer all agricultural land to industrial use
Reduce the total area under cultivation
questions.src: Settled post-independence land reform objective — abolition of Zamindari/Jagir/Inam systems aimed to remove intermediaries and establish direct state-cultivator relationships, aligned with Directive Principles under Article 39

questions.q: 'Conferment of ownership on tenants/ryots' as a land reform measure generally refers to:
o: Reducing tenants to landless labourers
Legislative measures granting tenants/cultivating ryots ownership rights over the land they cultivate, subject to conditions, as part of the broader tenancy reform movement
Increasing the rent payable by tenants
Abolishing all tenancy arrangements without providing any alternative rights
questions.src: Settled tenancy reform principle — various state tenancy laws conferred ownership rights on tenant-cultivators as part of the 'land to the tiller' reform philosophy following independence

questions.q: The full title of the 2013 central land acquisition legislation reflects its expanded scope beyond mere acquisition. It is known as:
o: The Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (unchanged)
The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013
The Land Reforms Act, 2013
The Eminent Domain Act, 2013
questions.src: The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (RFCTLARR Act) — replaced the colonial-era Land Acquisition Act 1894, adding rehabilitation/resettlement and fairer compensation provisions

questions.q: Under the RFCTLARR Act 2013, before land is acquired for certain categories of projects, the law generally requires:
o: No prior process at all — land can be acquired immediately upon notification
A Social Impact Assessment (SIA) study and, for private/PPP projects, the consent of a specified percentage of affected landowners, among other procedural safeguards
Only a newspaper advertisement, with no further formality
Approval from a foreign government
questions.src: RFCTLARR Act 2013 — introduces Social Impact Assessment requirements and consent thresholds (typically 70-80% for PPP/private projects) as procedural safeguards, a significant departure from the 1894 Act

questions.q: Under the RFCTLARR Act 2013, if a landowner is dissatisfied with the compensation award determined in the acquisition process, they generally have recourse to:
o: No remedy is available under the Act
Reference to the civil court / designated Authority for determination of the amount of compensation, as part of the Act's dispute resolution framework
Only an appeal to the Prime Minister's Office
Automatic doubling of compensation without any process
questions.src: RFCTLARR Act 2013 — provides for reference to court/Authority for compensation disputes, continuing (with modifications) the reference mechanism found in the earlier 1894 Act framework

questions.q: The Telangana Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973 primarily aims to:
o: Increase the maximum landholding any individual/family can hold, with no upper limit
Impose a ceiling (maximum limit) on the extent of agricultural land that a person or family unit may hold, with surplus land liable to be taken over by the government for redistribution
Apply only to urban residential property
Abolish agricultural land ownership altogether
questions.src: Telangana Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973 — imposes ceiling limits on agricultural landholding, with surplus land subject to government acquisition and redistribution, a core land reform measure

questions.q: Land ceiling and other land reform legislation in India has historically often been included in the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution primarily in order to:
o: Make such laws automatically unconstitutional
Provide such laws a degree of protection from being challenged as violative of Fundamental Rights (particularly the erstwhile Article 31/right to property), under Article 31B
Ensure such laws apply only to Union Territories
Remove such laws from all judicial review permanently under all circumstances
questions.src: Constitution of India, Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule — laws placed in the Ninth Schedule historically received protection from challenge on Fundamental Rights grounds, though the Supreme Court (I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu, 2007) held such laws remain subject to basic structure review if enacted after 24 April 1973

questions.q: Articles 38 and 39 of the Constitution of India, relevant to land reform and ceiling legislation, fall under which Part of the Constitution?
o: Part III — Fundamental Rights
Part IV — Directive Principles of State Policy
Part IVA — Fundamental Duties
Part XVIII — Emergency Provisions
questions.src: Constitution of India, Part IV (Articles 36-51) — Directive Principles of State Policy; Articles 38 and 39 specifically address social/economic justice and equitable distribution of resources, including land, relevant to land reform legislation

questions.q: The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 primarily aims to:
o: Transfer all forest land to private commercial ownership

Recognise and vest forest rights and occupation in forest land for Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers who have been residing in such forests for generations, correcting historical injustice
Abolish all forest reserves in India
Apply exclusively to urban forest areas
questions.src: Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (Forest Rights Act) — recognises individual and community forest rights for tribal and traditional forest-dwelling communities

questions.q: 'Scheduled Areas Land Transfer Regulation' generally aims to:
o: Encourage unrestricted transfer/sale of tribal land to non-tribals
Restrict or regulate the transfer of land in Scheduled Areas from tribal to non-tribal persons, in order to protect tribal land rights and prevent exploitation/alienation of tribal land
Apply only to land transactions between the government and private companies
Abolish the concept of Scheduled Areas entirely
questions.src: Scheduled Areas Land Transfer Regulations (e.g., the Andhra Pradesh Scheduled Areas Land Transfer Regulation 1 of 1959, applicable to relevant Telangana Scheduled Areas) — restrict transfer of tribal land to non-tribals to protect tribal communities

questions.q: The Telangana Assigned Lands (Prohibition of Transfers) Act, 1977 primarily deals with:
o: Land purchased through open market transactions by any citizen

Land assigned by the government to landless poor persons (assignees) for cultivation, and prohibits/restricts such assignees from transferring (selling, mortgaging, gifting) the assigned land to third parties
Only commercial and industrial land
Land owned by religious trusts exclusively
questions.src: Telangana Assigned Lands (Prohibition of Transfers) Act, 1977 — prohibits transfer of government-assigned land by assignees, protecting landless-poor beneficiaries from losing their assigned land through sale/mortgage

questions.q: Under laws relating to assigned lands, if an assignee transfers assigned land in violation of the prohibition on transfer, the general legal consequence is that:
o: The transfer is automatically valid and binding on the government
The transfer is void, and the land is liable to be resumed (taken back) by the government, often without payment of compensation for the illegal transfer
The assignee gains additional land as a penalty against the government
No consequence follows since assigned land laws are merely advisory
questions.src: Settled principle under assigned-lands legislation (e.g., the Telangana Assigned Lands (Prohibition of Transfers) Act 1977) — unauthorised transfers are void, with resumption of land to the government as the consequence

questions.q: 'Special Tribunals' constituted for the resolution of certain categories of land disputes (e.g., under land reform or land ceiling legislation) generally serve the function of:
o: Replacing the Supreme Court of India entirely
Providing specialised, often faster adjudication of specific categories of land disputes falling within their statutory jurisdiction, as an alternative or supplement to ordinary civil courts
Handling only criminal land-related offences
Functioning exclusively as revenue-collection bodies with no adjudicatory power
questions.src: Settled principle — special tribunals under land legislation (e.g., Land Reforms Tribunals) provide specialised adjudication for specific land dispute categories as defined by the relevant statute, distinct from ordinary civil court jurisdiction

questions.q: 'Survey and sub-division of land' as a land administration function primarily relates to:
o: The process of officially measuring, mapping, and dividing land parcels for purposes of accurate record-keeping, taxation, and identification of individual holdings
A process used only for urban commercial buildings
A judicial process requiring Supreme Court approval for every parcel
A one-time historical exercise with no ongoing relevance
questions.src: Settled land administration principle — survey and sub-division functions ensure accurate demarcation, mapping, and record maintenance of land parcels, foundational to land titling and revenue administration

questions.q: Land may generally be classified in revenue/land records based on factors including:
o: Only the colour of the soil, with no other classification recognised
Nature of use (agricultural, non-agricultural), tenure (patta/assigned/government), and irrigation source/type, among other classificatory criteria maintained in land records
Only the political party in power at the time of survey
The nationality of the landowner's ancestors
questions.src: Settled land records principle — classification of land in revenue records is based on factors such as use, tenure type, and irrigation source, forming the basis for record-of-rights (ROR) maintenance

questions.q: Article 39(b) of the Constitution of India, a Directive Principle relevant to land reform, directs the State to ensure that:
o: All land is nationalised without exception
The ownership and control of material resources of the community are so distributed as best to subserve the common good
Land can never be redistributed under any circumstances
Only urban land is subject to state regulation
questions.src: Constitution of India, Article 39(b) — Directive Principle directing equitable distribution of material resources (including land) to subserve the common good, a foundational basis for land reform and ceiling legislation
